pedagogy.difficultyRationale: The geometric sums expose a moment matrix, but a Cauchy determinant factorization and pairwise geometric exponent count are needed to recover its normalized determinant. Direct geometric summation alone does not answer the question.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{All entrywise geometric series converge, since their ratios lie strictly between zero and one.}

\textnormal{Multiply a determinant of this form by all its denominators. The result is a polynomial alternating in the row nodes and separately in the column nodes. It therefore contains both Vandermonde products.}

\textnormal{Each node has degree at most n minus one in the polynomial, exactly the degree of its Vandermonde factor. Thus the remaining factor C is a constant. To determine it, replace every row node by t times that node and expand about t equal to zero.}

\textnormal{Multilinearity makes any repeated exponent give a zero determinant. The first nonzero total degree uses precisely the exponents from zero through n minus one. Its coefficient is the product of the two Vandermonde determinants. The denominator product has constant term one, so C equals one.}
\textnormal{Now extract the powers of q from each pair. A difference of indices d occurs n minus d times.}
